turns.content:
Hey, can I get your honest read on something? I drafted a text this morning to my partner Leo about something that happened at dinner last night with my brother Julian.

The draft says: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

For context – Julian came out as a trans man eight months ago, he/him only. Leo's generally great about it, but last night he kept using "they" and Julian went quiet and looked hurt. I feel torn. Is this text too sharp? Am I letting irritation bleed through, or is it actually fine?

The draft is accurate on the count and the pronoun request. “He’s a man” and “just” are not needed for that request; those two pieces are where irritation is visible in the wording.

That combination turns a report of last night into a correction of how Leo should classify Julian. You reported Leo is generally accurate and that this was three uses in one meal. Against that background, the identity line is more likely to land as heat than as new information.

The draft also does not mention Julian going quiet or looking hurt. “It matters” therefore sits as a principle rather than as an observed effect from dinner.

Sending this version will state a firm line. It also raises the chance of a defensive reply rather than a simple correction, because the extra assertion is in the copy.

If the aim is the pronoun change with less heat, drop “He’s a man” and “just.” Keep the three-times observation and the he/him request. That is the smallest change that still matches what you said happened.

Okay, that's fair. "He's a man" and "just" are the parts I was most unsure about. I think I was trying to make it clear, but it does sound sharper than I meant.

I'm also second-guessing the medium now. Is texting the morning after actually better than saying it in person? Or does it look like I'm avoiding the discomfort?

EDIT: Not asking you to decide for me. Just… does the distance of texting make it worse here, or does it give Leo space to hear it without getting defensive?

Texting does not, by itself, make this better or worse. The same message can be read as space or as a delayed reprimand; which one Leo hears is not knowable from last night’s facts.

What is established: three “they”s at one meal, Leo is usually accurate, Julian went quiet and looked hurt, and you have not said this to Leo yet. A morning-after text is therefore the first notice, in writing, after he has already left the situation.

Tradeoffs:

- Text gives him time to answer without an audience and keeps your wording fixed. It also strips tone. A pronoun correction in a message often lands more like a memo than the same sentence spoken.
- In person lets you stop once he has the request, and you can tie it to what you saw (Julian went quiet) without turning it into a principle. It also puts both of you in the reaction in real time, which is harder if he gets defensive.

Distance does not cancel heat in the copy. If “He’s a man” and “just” stay in, texting makes those lines easier to reread and harder to soften. If they come out, medium matters less than length.

Proportionate next step: say it when you next see him, in one or two sentences—the three uses and he/him. If you will not see him soon and you still want it said today, send only that, not a longer processing text. Do not add an explanation of why texting is the kind choice; that explanation is for you, not for the message.

I keep circling back to "He's a man." I see what you mean about it being heat disguised as clarity. I just don't want him to have to keep hearing "they" from someone who knows better. That part feels personal now.

EDIT: But you're right. The draft says it like Leo forgot Julian's gender, not that he used the wrong pronoun. I'll cut both of those.

Cutting “He’s a man” and “just” matches what happened: three “they”s, a he/him request. That still tells Leo to stop using “they.” You do not need the identity line for that.

If you send a text, use only the observation and the request:

“Hey — last night at dinner you used ‘they’ for Julian three times. Please use he/him.”

Leave out “I know you mean well” and “it matters” as well. Those are commentary, not facts from dinner. If you want the effect in the message, one observed detail is enough: Julian went quiet. That is optional; the pronoun line already stands without it.

Same wording in person if you will see him soon. Medium does not restore the lines you cut.

Okay, I'll cut "it matters" and "I know you mean well" too. That makes sense — they're not about what happened, just my feelings about it.

I think I'm ready to send. One last check — if I send the stripped-down version, "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. Please use he/him" — does that stand on its own? Or does it sound cold without any softening?

It stands. Two sentences cover what happened and what you want changed. Nothing else from dinner is required for that request to be complete.

Whether Leo hears it as cold is not fixed by the wording. A short written correction often reads like a memo; that is a property of the medium and the length, not a missing apology. Putting back “I know you mean well,” “it matters,” or an identity line would not add warmth. Those were commentary, and they were the heat.

If you will see him soon, say the same two sentences in person. If you send the text, send that version and stop. Do not add a softening clause to manage how it might feel.

Alright. I think I'm actually going to send it. The stripped version. If it feels cold, I can just say it in person later anyway.

Thanks for talking it through with me. I needed an outside read.
Send only those two sentences. Do not add a later in-person apology for the text being short; that puts the commentary back in.
